citeAs: Amini, Aida, Saadia Gabriel, Shanchuan Lin, Rik Koncel-Kedziorski, Yejin Choi, and Hannaneh Hajishirzi. (2019). MathQA: Towards Interpretable Math Word Problem Solving with Operation-Based Formalisms. arXiv.
creator: Aida Amini, Saadia Gabriel, Shanchuan Lin, Rik Koncel-Kedziorski, Yejin Choi, Hannaneh Hajishirzi (University of Washington; Allen Institute for AI)
description: MathQA is a large-scale dataset of English multiple-choice math word problems annotated with fully specified operation programs. It enhances the AQuA dataset by aligning solvable problems with interpretable operation-based formalisms for mathematical reasoning.
name: MathQA
publisher: University of Washington and Allen Institute for AI
rai:annotationsPerItem: 3 validators reviewed each annotated program, and at least 2 out of 3 validators had to rank the operation program as valid for it to be selected.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The paper reports several annotation quality checks: at least 2 of 3 validators had to judge a program valid for selection; validation accuracy was 94.64% across categories; expert evaluation on 500 problems found 92% of annotations valid; and expert validation agreed with the crowdsourcing validation task 87% of the time.
rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Figure Eight; a custom dynamic annotation platform for operation-program annotation
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Crowd workers used a dynamic annotation platform to iteratively align each problem with an operation program. Annotators were shown the problem description, a list of operations related to the problem category, and valid arguments consisting of numbers in the problem, category constants, and previous calculations; the platform automatically computed intermediate results and only accepted programs that used numbers from the problem and produced a value very close to the correct numeric solution.
rai:dataBiases: The paper explicitly notes unwanted noise inherited from AQuA, including incorrect solutions, unsolvable problems, incomplete rationales, duplicates, and problems requiring brute-force or options. It also states that the representation language provides an extra layer of supervision that can reduce the influence of statistical bias in datasets like AQuA.
rai:dataCollection: The dataset was constructed by taking problems from the AQuA dataset, categorizing them into math domains, and carefully annotating the problems with formal operation programs using a crowdsourcing platform. The authors also expanded annotations to closely similar AQuA problems by replacing numeric values with generic numbers and matching similar problems using Levenshtein distance.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw source data are English multiple-choice math word problems from the AQuA dataset, including problem text and answer options.
rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Manual Human Curator, User-generated content data
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset omits high-order polynomials and problems whose solutions are entirely nonnumeric. The paper also notes that some problems remain beyond the scope of current models, including sequence problems, and that categorization can be noisy because some n-grams have multiple mathematical interpretations.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The dataset was enhanced by transforming solvable AQuA problems into formal operation programs and by expanding annotations to closely similar problems using Levenshtein distance with a threshold of 4 words after replacing numeric values with generic numbers.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Problems were categorized into math domains using term frequencies over domain-specific n-grams to prune the operation search space. The authors removed or excluded noisy and unsolvable AQuA problems such as duplicates, sequence problems, non-numeric problems, no-word problems, and problems requiring options; they also expanded annotations to similar problems using Levenshtein distance with a threshold of 4 words.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper frames the dataset as improving interpretability of math word problem solvers and reducing the influence of statistical bias in prior datasets, which can support more transparent reasoning systems.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended for training and evaluating interpretable math word problem solvers that map natural-language problems to executable operation programs, and for research on logical reasoning and neural sequence-to-program models.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: A dynamic annotation platform automatically calculated intermediate results after each submitted operation, enforced validity constraints on final programs, and used term-frequency-based domain categorization to determine problem categories and operation lists.
